title: Something Bigger Than Myself
author: Lacey Stapleton
summary: Lacey Stapleton of the Humanitas Institute tells the story of Sarah, a graduate of Jackson Hole Classical Academy who is now a newly commissioned Army officer, to illustrate what classical education claims to form. The piece begins with a single shadow day in seventh grade that opened Sarah to great literature, memorized poetry, and Latin, and it insists that these studies are formative rather than ornamental. It then defends the classical practice of memorizing poetry, arguing that a poem learned by heart becomes part of a child and returns when courage, comfort, or wisdom is needed. The central image is Kipling's poem If, which Sarah memorized in class and later found posted on the barracks walls at West Point. Stapleton closes with the Augustinian claim that we become what we love, presenting Sarah's choice of service as the fruit of a well-ordered love and the aim of a classical education: a trained mind joined to a heart and will directed toward the good.
points: A single shadow day at a classical school, by the student's own account, taught her more than her previous seven years of schooling.
The article defends poetry memorization not as a party trick but as a way of making words part of a child that return in moments of testing.
Kipling's If, memorized in a classical classroom, reappeared on the barracks walls at West Point, tying school formation to adult vocation.
The argument rests on the claim that we become what we love, so education succeeds when it orders a student's loves toward courage, honesty, and discipline.
quotes: For Sarah, it started with a single day. In seventh grade, she spent one day shadowing at Jackson Hole Classical Academy. She says she learned more that day than in the seven years of school before it.
These studies aren’t ornaments. They formatively shape how a young person sees the world.

Parents often marvel when their child can recite a long poem from memory, but the point was never to impress people at parties. A poem learned by heart becomes part of a child. It stays with them for life, and it comes back when they need courage, comfort, or wisdom.
Years later, Sarah arrived at West Point to train as an Army officer. There, on the walls of the barracks, was the same poem.
We become what we love. Through years of stories, poems, and lessons, Sarah’s imagination filled with images of courage, honesty, and discipline, until she came to love those things for herself.
It is what a classical education hopes to form in every child: not only a well-trained mind, but a heart that loves what is good and a will ready to act on it.
